_comment: SAMPLE bundle. Demonstrates the FULL contract shape (systems × parameter-configurations × metrics) for an arbitrary, open set of suites. Four suites carry real (stale, pre-VPS) local numbers; the other four are structurally complete but results-pending. This file is for design validation; the ACTIVE default (results.json) renders everything PENDING until the VPS run lands. See ../../RESULTS_INJECTION_GUIDE.md.

provenance.note: Sample: real local numbers for 4 suites; the rest awaiting the VPS run. NOT final.

suites.label: SmartLoad vs plain NGINX
suites.question: Does SmartLoad's full decision plane beat plain NGINX round-robin on the same hardware, workload, and backend pool?
suites.summary: A/B comparison (#148): identical 5-backend pool and Locust load; only the decision plane (forecasting + anomaly-aware routing + autoscaling) is toggled between the two sides, which run serially. Broken down by load phase.

provenance.note: No committed run yet — awaiting the VPS benchmark.

suites.label: Adaptive scaling (RQ4)
suites.question: Does forecast-driven scale-out keep latency and errors flat as load ramps, spikes, and an anomaly hits?
suites.summary: Single-stack demonstration across a five-phase load curve (bootstrap → forecast burst → sustain → anomaly scale-down → steady), measuring how the pool grows ahead of saturation and recovers. One system, broken down by phase.

provenance.note: No committed run yet — awaiting the VPS benchmark.

suites.label: RL routing (honest null result)
suites.question: Does the trained PPO routing policy beat classical load-balancing baselines on tail latency and SLA-violation, across backend scenarios?
suites.summary: Closed-loop causal M/G/c simulation, 5 eval seed-bands × 40 episodes × 128 windows. Ranking key is p95 + SLA-violation (lower is better); reward is diagnostic only. Broken down by backend scenario.

verdict.text: PPO trails the classical baselines on latency and SLA-violation; least-response-time leads. Shadow only.

metrics.label: SLA-violation
metrics.hint: Fraction of windows over the 200 ms SLA

charts.title: p95 latency by router (homogeneous)
charts.note: Lower is better. The emphasised bar is the leader — a classical policy, not the PPO router.

charts.title: SLA-violation by router (homogeneous)
charts.note: The PPO policy violates the 200 ms SLA roughly twice as often as round-robin — the honest finding behind demoting it to shadow.

suites.label: Autoscaler strategy
suites.question: Does the target controller beat the previous ±1 rule, the naive threshold, and static provisioning, across load shapes?
suites.summary: Provisioning strategies on the same per-(profile, seed) demand realisation; every dynamic strategy calls the shipped decide rule, only the controller and signal change. Aggregate plus per-profile breakdown.

verdict.text: Target controller lifts SLA 77.2% → 98.3% on the same forecast — past the old oracle (95.5%).

charts.title: SLA% by strategy (all profiles)
charts.note: Higher is better. The controller, on the same MA signal, clears the old perfect-foresight oracle.

charts.title: SLA% by profile — controller vs old rule
charts.note: The lift holds across every load shape.

suites.label: Forecasting engine
suites.question: Does the candidate forecaster beat the shipped moving-average and the persistence floor on next-bucket accuracy, across load shapes?
suites.summary: Single-step (next 5-min bucket) forecast accuracy, rolling-origin / walk-forward, 5 seeds × 4 profiles. Every engine is handed the identical history window at each origin. Aggregate plus per-profile.

verdict.text: Harmonic-residual wins every error metric (MAPE 5.4% vs 10.5%) and is the only calibrated band.

charts.title: MAPE by engine (all profiles)
charts.note: Lower is better. Harmonic-residual beats the shipped moving-average and the persistence floor.

charts.title: MAPE by load profile
charts.note: Moving-average degrades badly on the diurnal and spiky shapes; harmonic-residual stays low across all four.

suites.label: Forecasting downstream
suites.question: Does a forward-projecting forecast deliver real end-to-end SLA value over a reactive trailing mean, across load shapes?
suites.summary: Each strategy drives the same shipped autoscaler decide rule in the same warm-up-aware loop; only the scalar signal differs, so any SLA gap is the forecast's. Aggregate plus per-profile, 8 seeds × 6 profiles.

verdict.text: HR’s 20-second projection adds +6.3 pp SLA over reactive; the moving-average adds nothing.

charts.title: End-to-end SLA% by scaling signal (all profiles)
charts.note: Reactive and the shipped moving-average coincide to the digit — the MA carries no forward lead. HR projects ahead and gains.

charts.title: Where forecasting pays — HR SLA gain vs reactive
charts.note: The forecast pays most on the structured shapes (sawtooth, diurnal, ramp); on near-random spikes there is nothing to lead.

suites.label: Anomaly detection quality
suites.question: Which detector best identifies real anomalies (precision / recall / F1), and how much does the stability gate help, across injection profiles?
suites.summary: Six detectors scored on identical ground-truth-labelled synthetic traces (latency spikes, error bursts, gradual degradation, clean controls, plus held-out partial-failure and flappy-clean). Broken down by injection profile. Distinct from the engine-agreement bench: this measures detection quality on labelled sequences.

provenance.note: No committed run yet — awaiting the VPS benchmark.

suites.label: Engine agreement (decision surface)
suites.question: Where does the trained IsolationForest's decision boundary agree with — and diverge from — the simple threshold rule across the feature space?
suites.summary: Both engines scored at every cell of a latency × error-rate feature grid. This measures decision-surface agreement, not detection quality — a sanity check on the production scaler and where the model adds or loses signal. Distinct from the detection-quality bench.

provenance.note: No committed run yet — awaiting the VPS benchmark.

kpis.label: Engine agreement
kpis.hint: share of grid cells with matching verdicts

audit.title: Control-loop audit & hardening
audit.summary: Read-only code audit cross-checked against the live stack and on-disk bench artifacts, plus a fresh before/after benchmark. Each candidate root-cause was handed to an independent reviewer whose job was to refute it.

verdict.text: A coupled autoscaler-flap + no-recovery-trap drove the storms; five fixes cut errors 54.5% → 0.39% (~140×).

stages.label: D1 alone
stages.note: exposed the coupling — D1 alone made it worse

stages.label: D1+D2+D3 (max=5 saturation bench)
stages.note: deliberate saturation design, not a bug

stages.label: + spike hardening
stages.note: all 3 runs 0.03–0.89%, active pool never below 4

items.label: Autoscaler asymmetric demand signal → pool flap
items.detail: Scale-out was sized on max(predicted, offered) but scale-in on predicted alone — a permanent 4↔5 flap dead-zone. Both directions now size on the same demand band.

items.label: Sidecar no-recovery trap
items.detail: A benched backend gets no traffic → emits no metrics → the detector never re-publishes healthy, so it stays benched forever. Recovery is now driven off registry membership.

items.label: Detector latency channel over-exclusion
items.detail: A load-driven latency ramp was scored as illness, cascading into pool collapse. A margin-primary peer-suppressor now downgrades a rising-together cohort to advisory.

items.label: Spike-transient hardening
items.detail: Exclusion hysteresis + surge suppression keep the active pool from collapsing during a spike.

items.label: Prime suspect: lb-sidecar is the root cause
items.detail: REFUTED — the sidecar holds no Docker lifecycle authority; it is the actuator and recovery bottleneck, not the originator of the storm.

items.label: Kubernetes deferred during the measurement phase
items.detail: HPA / readiness probes would silently replace the very components under study (RL routing, peer-relative exclusion, forecast-band scaling), confounding the experiment.
